chapter: New York, Henderson and Charlie Johnson
title: Why so few women brass players: Dyer Jones, Dolly Jones, Leora, Mary Lou Williams
summary: Asked about women brass players, he says he saw none until Dyer Jones, never heard Leora play, and pays tribute to Mary Lou Williams on piano.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: You know, Herman, this reminds me. We've just mentioned three women trumpet players. We mentioned Dyer Jones, Dottie Jones, and now Leora Henderson.
Yeah.
And yet there are so few women in brass players, or reed players. Why is that, in jazz?

I don't know, because to me there's no such animal, until I met Dyer. I'd never heard of a -- well, you saw -- when I was a kid you'd see a woman who played piano, played in church. Ding, ding-da-ding. Church piano. You know what I mean. They -- 'Come to Jesus,' I mean that's a song that we always -- [Mamie] always said, it didn't sound like anything. And later years, I mean all the way up to Mary Lou Williams.
Right.
Nobody could play piano with anybody respected until her. I didn't. And a heck of a lot of people didn't. You know. That chick, she didn't care about it still
today. She don't care about a lot of the men, you know, Mary Lou Williams.
(Laughter.)
I mean when it comes to playing piano. But they'd sit down, ti-dee, ti-dee, ta-dee, you're sorry you saw your lesson, you know.
But is there -- is there -- so far as women are concerned, and a brass instrument, is there a problem that the wind volume, or --
Well --
What is it?

Considerably, I would say yes, but I mean that's what everyone thought. Neither one of those women played like Herman played. I mean not with the fire. But Dyer hit those high notes right on -- them G's, right on the head, with no trouble. Now I never heard --
Leora?
Leora play. I never heard her hit a note.
Oh, you never did?

I never did, because I -- by reputation, see? And I heard her brother play some songs that sounded doggone good to me, big round tones, and pretty changes, sitting in a London club. There were rehearsals I heard some of his, 'bah ti bah te bee bah bo, bee bah,' let me know that she
knew what she was doing, you know? 'Bah bo bee bah bah,' they'd play one of those things. But -- that's the way I see it. That's the way I say. Maybe I'm wrong. I mean that's what I heard. You know.
Yeah.
Uh-huh.
